Pregnancy

Rheumatoid arthritis and birth: planning your delivery

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Many people with rheumatoid arthritis can give birth vaginally. The safest plan depends on your pregnancy, disease activity, joint movement, medicines and preferences: not the diagnosis alone. Discuss these together with your maternity and rheumatology teams before labour.

What rheumatoid arthritis means for pregnancy

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune illness that inflames the lining of joints. Pain, swelling and prolonged morning stiffness often affect the hands, wrists and feet; fatigue and reduced movement can make daily tasks harder. Long-standing inflammation can damage joints, and some people also have eye, skin, lung or heart involvement.

RA is more common in women, but it does not automatically mean infertility or an inability to carry a pregnancy. It is different from ordinary joint wear and from axial spondyloarthritis. Your actual joints, organ involvement and previous operations matter more for birth planning than a general label such as rheumatism.

Aim for control, not a promise of improvement

If possible, discuss pregnancy while disease activity is low or in remission and treatment is stable. Planning may take several months because medicines and monitoring sometimes need changing. There is no single waiting period that makes every pregnancy safe; an unplanned pregnancy needs prompt review rather than blame.

Symptoms sometimes improve during pregnancy, but this is not a cure or a reason to stop treatment. Recent cohorts of well-treated patients often show stable control, with flares still possible after birth. Active disease is associated with complications such as premature birth or a smaller baby; an association does not mean these outcomes are inevitable or that caesarean birth prevents them.

Review medicines before conception and early in pregnancy

Bring the exact names and doses of prescriptions, painkillers and supplements. Pregnancy-compatible treatments can include hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine and selected biologic medicines, including TNF inhibitors, when appropriate. Untreated inflammation also has risks; do not stop all medicines because you are pregnant.

Methotrexate used for RA must not be taken during pregnancy. Arrange a specialist change before trying to conceive: UK advice often describes at least three months, while some current US labels require six months of contraception after the last dose. Follow the plan for your exact medicine and circumstances, not a universal online interval. If pregnancy occurs during treatment, contact the prescriber promptly before another dose. Other drugs, such as leflunomide or JAK inhibitors, also need specific review.

Make a medicine plan for labour

Do not abruptly stop long-term oral steroids. Some people need additional steroid cover during labour or surgery, depending on their usual treatment and adrenal function. The team should document this and decide any changes to biologic treatment around delivery; there is no single schedule for all injections.

Check pain medicines separately. Avoid self-directed NSAIDs such as ibuprofen from 20 weeks of pregnancy unless a clinician specifically advises them; later pregnancy has additional restrictions. Prescribed low-dose aspirin is a different situation and should not be stopped on this advice. Record anticoagulants too, because dose timing can affect an epidural or spinal anaesthetic.

Does RA mean a caesarean is safer?

No. Vaginal birth is often possible, and RA alone is not an indication for caesarean delivery. Studies may report more caesareans among people with RA, but this does not show that routinely choosing surgery improves outcomes. Consider the baby’s position, placenta, fetal wellbeing, labour progress and your individual medical condition.

A caesarean may be recommended for an obstetric reason or when particular functional limitations make vaginal birth unsuitable. It is major surgery with risks such as infection, bleeding and blood clots, and it can add to recovery needs. Discuss your preferences and the benefits and disadvantages of each realistic option; pre-eclampsia does not automatically mean that caesarean is the only route.

Plan positions around your comfortable movement

Painful hips, knees, wrists or shoulders can limit positions, but do not assume they rule out labour. A midwife and physiotherapist can help you try supported positions before birth. Side-lying, pillows or other supports may help some people; avoid forcing a joint beyond its comfortable range.

Document any hip replacement, restricted movement or painful position. A hip replacement alone does not automatically require a caesarean. When an epidural reduces sensation, staff still need to respect your movement limits and support your legs and other joints; reduced pain does not make excessive stretching safe.

An epidural is not automatically excluded

RA does not by itself make an epidural or spinal anaesthetic impossible. Arrange an antenatal anaesthetic discussion if you have major movement limits, spinal disease or surgery, previous difficult anaesthesia, blood-clotting problems or anticoagulant treatment. The clinician assesses the actual anatomy and risks.

An epidural can provide effective labour pain relief but may need adjustment and does not always work fully. Other options include breathing and relaxation support, gas and air, and medicines offered by the maternity service. Discuss a backup plan rather than assuming either that pain relief is guaranteed or that general anaesthesia is the only alternative.

Tell the anaesthetist about your neck, jaw and breathing

RA can sometimes affect the upper neck joints, jaw opening or joints around the voice box. Tell the team about known neck instability, neck symptoms, restricted mouth opening, persistent hoarseness, swallowing problems or breathing symptoms. These details can affect safe positioning and airway management.

General anaesthesia also needs careful planning when the airway or neck is affected. The anaesthetist decides whether examination, previous records or further tests are needed; not everyone needs the same scans. Do not force your neck into a position to test it yourself, and do not assume that lumbar back pain explains every cervical or airway problem.

Write down a practical birth plan

Agree who coordinates maternity, rheumatology and anaesthetic care, and how to reach them if labour starts early or disease flares. Include useful positions, movement limits, pain-relief preferences, medicine instructions, steroid needs, the last anticoagulant dose if relevant, and a plan if surgery becomes necessary.

Bring an up-to-date medicine list and relevant operation or anaesthetic records. Ask about help getting out of bed, using the toilet, holding and feeding the baby, and lifting safely when hands or hips are sore. A birth plan records preferences and medical needs while leaving room for changes if you or your baby need different care.

Prepare for recovery and a possible flare

Arrange rheumatology follow-up after birth rather than waiting until symptoms become disabling. Fatigue, sleep disruption and a flare can make recovery harder. Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and practical help with baby care can reduce painful strain; discuss suitable feeding supports and accessible equipment.

Your team should reassess blood-clot risk, especially after surgery, reduced mobility or a hospital stay. Movement within your limits and any prescribed prevention need an individual plan. If you use heparin or another anticoagulant, get written instructions for labour, anaesthesia and restarting treatment; do not calculate or change the timing yourself.

Coordinate treatment and feeding after birth

Breastfeeding is possible with many RA treatments, including several conventional and biologic medicines. Compatibility depends on the exact drug and dose, the baby’s health and the available alternatives. Arrange any restart or change in advance so that neither uncontrolled disease nor an unsupported feeding decision is forced on you.

Methotrexate illustrates why specialist advice matters: some labels advise against breastfeeding, while current European guidance allows consideration of low weekly doses only when no alternative exists. Do not start it while breastfeeding on the basis of this article. Tell the baby’s clinician about biologic exposure during pregnancy before live vaccines are given; recommendations vary with the medicine, exposure timing and vaccine, rather than requiring every vaccine to be delayed.

Do not assume every new symptom is an RA flare

Get urgent clinical assessment for sudden severe pain in one joint, new joint swelling or colour change, difficulty moving a joint, or joint pain with fever, chills or feeling unwell. Joint infection can be serious, particularly with immune-suppressing treatment, and fever is not always present. Do not increase steroids yourself to cover an unexplained new problem.

Seek emergency help for sudden unexplained breathing difficulty, chest pain or tightness, coughing blood, fainting or loss of consciousness, or a seizure. New severe neurological symptoms or thoughts of harming yourself also need immediate help. Do not drive yourself in an emergency. Tell the clinician that you are pregnant or recently gave birth and list your medicines.

Know the maternity warning signs

Contact maternity care immediately for a severe or worsening headache, new visual changes, pain below the ribs, sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet, heartburn that does not improve with medicine, vomiting or feeling very unwell. Pre-eclampsia can occur during pregnancy or after birth; these symptoms should not be explained away as joint disease or medication effects.

Other urgent warnings include a temperature of 38°C or more, new breathlessness, a racing or irregular heartbeat, severe abdominal pain that starts suddenly, persists or worsens, one-sided limb pain or swelling, vaginal bleeding or fluid leakage, or your baby moving less than usual. Heavy bleeding after birth needs immediate help. Do not wait for several signs or the next appointment; use emergency services if symptoms are severe, you faint or you cannot reach urgent maternity help.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Delivery route and anaesthesia should be planned around your individual pregnancy, disease activity, function and medicines.

Ask for written instructions covering medicines, comfortable positions, urgent contacts, recovery and feeding.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to prepare your medicine list, joint movement limits, previous anaesthetic details and questions for the birth-planning appointment. It cannot select your delivery route, assess anaesthetic safety or change a prescription; recording symptoms must never delay urgent care.

When to seek help

RA alone is not a reason to choose surgery or stop all medicines. Seek emergency help without driving yourself for sudden unexplained breathing difficulty, chest pain, coughing blood, fainting or a seizure. Maternity warning signs and new severe joint symptoms need prompt clinical assessment; do not wait for several signs or assume they are a flare.

Evidence notes updated: November 4, 2026

Key takeaways

  • RA alone does not require a caesarean or rule out an epidural.
  • Disease control and pregnancy-compatible treatment protect both maternal health and birth planning.
  • Joint movement, neck or jaw problems and anticoagulants need individual anaesthetic assessment.
  • Write down medicine, positioning, recovery, feeding and infant-vaccine plans before birth.
  • New joint infection signs or maternity warning symptoms need prompt assessment, not an assumed flare.

Frequently asked questions

Can I have a vaginal birth with RA?

Often, yes. The decision depends on obstetric factors, your joint function and overall health, and your preferences. More caesareans in some RA studies do not prove that everyone benefits from planned surgery.

Will labour necessarily be more painful?

Not necessarily. Joint pain and limited movement can make some positions uncomfortable, so plan support and pain relief in advance. Labour experience varies; neither painless birth nor unusually severe pain can be predicted from RA alone.

Can hip damage or a replacement prevent vaginal birth?

Severe limitations may affect the plan, but a damaged or replaced hip does not automatically exclude vaginal birth. Assess comfortable movement and supported positions before labour, and protect those limits even when sensation is reduced.

Does spinal involvement mean I cannot have an epidural?

No automatic rule applies. An anaesthetist reviews the location of the problem, prior surgery, positioning, clotting and medicines. Upper-neck or airway problems also matter for general anaesthesia and should be discussed beforehand.

Should I stop RA medicines during pregnancy?

Do not stop all treatment. Some drugs are compatible and others require a planned switch. Methotrexate for RA is not suitable in pregnancy; contact your prescriber promptly if pregnancy occurs while taking it. Never abruptly stop long-term oral steroids.

Does pregnancy make RA disappear?

No. Some people improve, others remain stable or flare, and symptoms can increase after birth. Continue the agreed monitoring and treatment plan even if your joints feel better.

Can I breastfeed and restart treatment?

Often there are compatible options, but the exact medicine, dose and baby’s circumstances need review. Agree a plan with rheumatology and maternity care before delivery; also tell the baby’s clinician about pregnancy exposure to biologic medicines before live vaccines.

Which symptoms should not wait?

Sudden unexplained breathing difficulty, chest pain, coughing blood, fainting or a seizure need emergency help without self-driving. Contact maternity care immediately for severe or worsening headache, vision changes, pain below the ribs, sudden swelling or unrelieved heartburn, fever of 38°C or more, severe abdominal pain, reduced fetal movement, bleeding or fluid leakage. A sudden painful or swollen joint also needs urgent assessment; do not assume a flare.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
